idh.reasoning: The strongest metadata favoring an IDH-mutant diffuse glioma are the young age and cortically based temporal/parietal involvement, with only mild enhancement and very small necrotic/non-enhancing core relative to the whole tumor. These features fit better with an IDH-mutant glioma than with the more typical older-patient, frankly necrotic/enhancing IDH-wildtype pattern. Against this, the very large edema burden, measurable enhancing tumor, ventricular/ependymal invasion, deep white-matter invasion, midline shift, and absence of a T2-FLAIR mismatch pattern all reduce specificity and raise concern for a more aggressive IDH-wildtype phenotype. Balancing these conflicting features, the age and cortical hemispheric distribution slightly outweigh the aggressive imaging features, so the best MRI-based estimate is IDH-mutant with limited confidence.

one_p_nineteen_q.reasoning: For 1p/19q status, the metadata do not provide highly specific markers. Features supporting a non-codeleted diffuse glioma include substantial edema, measurable enhancing tumor, ependymal/ventricular invasion, deep white-matter invasion, and mass effect, which are less typical for classic lower-grade oligodendroglioma morphology. Temporal/parietal location is also less stereotypical than the classic frontal-predominant oligodendroglioma pattern, although location alone is weak evidence. Arguing against non-codeletion, the patient is young, the tumor has cortical involvement, and enhancement is described as mild, all of which can be seen in oligodendroglioma. Because the evidence is indirect and conflicting, the best estimate is non-codeleted with low-to-moderate confidence.

overall_comment: MRI metadata alone cannot definitively determine molecular subtype or WHO grade; tissue diagnosis with molecular testing is required. The main uncertainty is the tension between young age and cortical hemispheric location favoring IDH-mutant disease versus edema, enhancement, ventricular involvement, and mass effect suggesting aggressive biology.

who_grade.reasoning: For WHO grade, the imaging metadata strongly favor a high-grade lesion rather than grade 2 because there is measurable contrast-enhancing tumor, a necrotic/non-enhancing core component, thick enhancing margin, extensive edema, ventricular/ependymal invasion, deep white-matter invasion, and midline shift. These features collectively support grade 4 more than grade 3, especially the necrotic component and marked mass effect. Arguing against grade 4, enhancement is described as mild, the necrotic proportion is very small, and the measured enhancing/necrotic core is not overwhelmingly large compared with the whole tumor. Nevertheless, the combination of enhancement, necrotic component, ependymal/deep invasion, extensive edema, and mass effect makes CNS WHO grade 4 the best MRI-based estimate.
